summary: Weekly POC check-in focused on results from last weekend's burst run, tuning autoscale thresholds, and planning an upcoming 2-hour stress rehearsal. Team agreed to try a conservative min-replica bump and shorter cooldowns; Redwood to send explicit JSON and cost tradeoffs.
topics: burst test readout; autoscale policy tweaks (min/max replicas, scale step, cooldown); KV/prefix cache behavior; fallback routes to hosted model; private deployment security asks; cost vs latency tradeoff
questions: Can we shorten cooldown without oscillation?; Is 2x min replicas needed for cold-start heavy workflows?; What are failure modes during cross-region bursts?
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-15 14:05 PST - duration 47m - recording. Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Omar (Redwood SE), Jules (Redwood SRE Advocate), Priya (Redwood SE), Lena (BrightPath), Samir (SRE), Ayesha (CTO), Diego (ML Eng), Ivy (Security).

Summary: quick recap of last weekend's burst rehearsal, observed tail latencies and cache hit rates, propose autoscale tuning and one more formal stress run.

[00:00] Maya: Okay folks, thanks for joining, we'll do a 45 minute sync — quick readout from the weekend's test then focus on autoscale tuning and next steps. Sorry if audio is a bit crunchy.
[00:12] Lena: No problem, thanks, Maya. We ran the scheduled burst from 10pm to midnight Saturday, simulated 3.5k concurrent active sessions hitting the chat endpoint. We saw an initial spike, then a plateau but tail p99 got a bit rough, like 1.8s to 2.6s on some sequences.
[00:35] Omar: Can you remind us of the current pilot config? I have it as min_replicas=1, max_replicas=8, scale_step=2, cooldown=180s and the model is redwood-davinci-13b-quant (note: SE said 'red-wood davinci' in transcript).
[00:48] Samir: Yep that's right, and we also had prefix cache enabled but initial KV cache warmup was slow. Hit-rate only reached ~36% after 20 minutes, which explains some of the repeated long tails when workers cold started.
[01:10] Priya: Right, with min_replicas=1 you get a lot of cold starts under a fast ramp. One of the levers is to raise min_replicas to 2 or 3 to keep KV caches warm and reduce per-request latency. Also shorten cooldown to 60s so scale responds faster to load - but that increases oscillation risk.
[01:34] Ayesha: What's the expected cost delta if we bump min_replicas to 2? Our goal is 99th < 1s for short chats, acceptable average cost increase up to 20%.
[01:49] Maya: We'll calc a back-of-envelope. For this instance type and our token mix, doubling min_replicas roughly adds ~28% cost on steady baseline; but if burst windows are frequent it can reduce total token processing time and therefore lower some tail cost due to fewer replays. Omar, can you run numbers?
[02:07] Omar: Yep, I'll run the estimate and share. Also want to call out prefix caching: we observed a lot of similar conversation starts so increasing prefix cache bucket size and TTL might lift hit-rate from 36% to ~65% — that materially lowers per-token GPU compute.
[02:28] Diego: Quick question, is prefix cache here the one in the Redwood runtime or our application-level cache? I thought we had both.
[02:36] Jules: Good point, there's app-level and runtime-level. The runtime KV cache is the one helping decode K V cache hits on token generation. Sometimes transcript engines show it as K V cash or K V cache, but it's the runtime one we tuned.
[02:54] Samir: On failures: we saw two worker OOMs around the 10 minute mark into burst. Memory pressure seemed correlated with concurrent long-sequence requests — a few users submitted long docs that pinned KV and pushed memory. We fell back to a lower-capacity model for a short window and that restored throughput but increased latencies.
[03:18] Priya: That suggests autoscale step=2 may be too small for sudden jumps with long sequences. Increasing scale_step to 3 for the pilot bursts and adding a short, pro-active surge policy (pre-scale when CPU or queue length crosses threshold) could prevent that.
[03:36] Lena: We're concerned about oscillation though. If we scale up aggressively and then scale down too quickly we might ping-pong.
[03:44] Omar: Use staggered cooldown: aggressive scale-up cooldown 20s for detection and a longer scale-down cooldown 180s. Or better: scale-down only when sustained below threshold for two intervals. That way you avoid rapid downscales.
[04:01] Ayesha: Is there a built-in hysteresis or is that manual policy?
[04:07] Priya: Redwood's Dedicated runtime supports policy rules with hysteresis (they call it hold-time and stable-intervals in the UI) — but the naming in logs sometimes shows up as 'hold' or 'hld' in auto transcribed notes. We'll send the exact fields.
[04:22] Diego: Also curious about fallback to hosted model — we saw a switch to the hosted endpoint once when a node fail happened. How transparent is that in terms of data residency and request routing?
[04:33] Maya: Good question — fallback routing is configurable. For the POC you have it set to failover to Redwood hosted for capacity; that does cross traffic to the hosted environment and is subject to the hosted retention policy. Ivy, that ties into your security question.
[04:46] Ivy: Yes, for us any cross-tenant hosted fallback requires additional compliance review. We need a decision: do we want fallback allowed for production? For the POC we can enable with logging but we need an audited trail and KMS integration for keys.
[05:02] Maya: Noted. We'll include the hosted-fallback config and the audit-logging behavior in the security doc we share.
[05:12] Samir: Back to tuning — what about shorter sequence batching? A lot of latency came from long-sequence outliers. Could we isolate long runs to a separate queue/instance pool?
[05:23] Omar: Yes, route long-sequence requests to a separate pool (we call it a slow-path pool) with larger memory GPUs. It costs more but keeps the normal pool optimized for short chats. We can set the routing policy by request metadata (token_count > X).
[05:40] Lena: That would help; our main workload is short chats but we do have long-polling sessions occasionally.
[05:47] Priya: For the pilot we recommend two practical changes: bump min_replicas to 2, adjust scale_step to 3 for bursts, shorten scale-up cooldown to 20s, and add a short surge pre-warm rule that triggers when queue length > 200 for 15s. Also increase prefix cache TTL from 5m to 30m for these identical conversation starts.
[06:10] Diego: Any risk with cache TTL causing staleness? We sometimes have model prompt updates that we want to pick up quickly.
[06:16] Omar: You can invalidate prefix cache per-deployment on config change; TTL is just a standby — so safe for the pilot.
[06:24] Ayesha: Ok sounds reasonable. Can we get a concrete JSON example of that autoscale policy?
[06:29] Maya: Yes — action item, I'll send that with annotated rationale.
[06:34] [06:34] Short pause while Maya shares a screen and a quick deck.
[07:02] Maya: Screen: sample policy. I know transcripts sometimes garble the names — there's a minReplicas, maxReplicas, step, cooldownUp, cooldownDown, surgeRules array. I'll paste the JSON in the follow-up.
[07:21] Samir: One more data point from the run: average GPU utilization peaked at 72% during the plateau but the variance was high — some replicas were at 95% while others idle — suggests load wasn't evenly balanced.
[07:35] Jules: That can be due to request routing sticky behavior or uneven queue distribution. The runtime supports continuous batching that should better spread. We'll check batching thresholds and worker affinity.
[07:49] Lena: Also curious about how dedicated capacity burst pooling works — is that reserved GPUs we can burst to or is it shared?
[07:58] Priya: For Dedicated you get a pool for your org; burst capacity can be a separate overflow capacity that may be multi-tenant and subject to SLAs. For strict isolation you choose reserved capacity. We'll put definitions in the doc.
[08:14] Ayesha: Cost question again — how much does burst overflow cost versus reserved?
[08:20] Maya: Overflow tends to have a premium of roughly 1.4x on per-minute GPU cost; reserved is cheaper but requires commit. We'll include a table in the follow-up.
[08:30] Diego: On the OOMs — do we have a heap dump or a trace?
[08:35] Omar: We captured a JVM-ish trace from the worker (some logs lost due to rotation, transcript picks up 'rot-ation' as 'rotten') but we have the process memstats. We'll share the excerpt; it shows concurrent max mem at 93% right before OOM.
[08:53] Samir: We'll try to reproduce in a targeted repro with long sequences, but that may take time.
[09:01] Maya: Plan for the next test — a formal 2-hour stress rehearsal with pre-warm and separate long-seq pool. Customer to run it next Wednesday at 10pm, Redwood to monitor and have on-call SEs.
[09:12] Lena: Confirmed. We also want Redwood to instrument a short dashboard tile with queue length, per-replica utilization, and prefix cache hit rate.
[09:22] Jules: We can add that in the Console as a temporary dashboard during the POC.
[09:28] Ivy: One security flag — we need to ensure logs include request IDs and are TTLed per our retention policy. Also we want KMS integration and an answer on whether keys ever leave our VPC in fallback scenarios.
[09:41] Maya: We'll document KMS behavior; keys do not leave customer-managed KMS when Private is used, but hosted fallback uses Redwood-managed KMS unless you opt-out. We'll be explicit.
[09:56] Ayesha: Could you also provide the SLA behavior if we hit 99.9 latency SLOs? We need to see expected degradation and the failover model.
[10:05] Priya: SLA language is in the enterprise docs — we'll pull the relevant excerpt and annotate it for the pilot.
[10:13] Samir: For final tuning, I want to run one more micro-burst test: 5-minute ramp to 4k QPS then hold 30 minutes, with the long-seq pool seeded with 10% of traffic. This should expose the scaling step behavior.
[10:28] Omar: Good plan. We'll on our side run a shadow test to measure latency without affecting production.
[10:33] Maya: Ok recap. Action items: Maya send autoscale JSON + cost table; Omar share cache hit-rate report and memstat excerpt; Samir run the micro-burst pattern and share exact QPS curve; Ivy list compliance docs for private fallback. We'll meet after the big rehearsal to review results.
[10:54] Ayesha: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
[11:00] Maya: Thanks, we'll follow up in email with links: autoscale JSON, security doc, and proposed test window.

End of meeting.

Notes on transcript quality: several product names transcribed imperfectly (e.g., 'red-wood davinci', 'K V cash'), timestamps approximate, speaker labels sometimes shorthand.
